questions.prompt: Column D was imported from a system that preserves leading zeros by exporting quantities as text. Running =SUM(D2:D10) over it returns a number smaller than a manual total. Why?
options: SUM adds only genuine numeric values, so any cell whose quantity is stored as text is invisible to it, even though it displays identically to a real number
SUM rounds every value down before adding, which cancels out variation in the decimal places added
SUM throws #VALUE! for the whole range the moment it meets a text cell, so the displayed total is actually a cached result from an earlier calculation
SUM only works correctly inside an Excel Table, never on a plain range like D2:D10
questions.explain: SUM adds only genuine numeric values; a cell holding "1024" as text is invisible to SUM even though it displays identically to a real number — exactly the silent gotcha Lesson 2 warns about. Converting the text-stored values with VALUE(), or using the Convert to Number fix, resolves it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside an Excel Table, a ________ like Table1[Sales] refers to a column by name instead of a fixed cell address, and keeps meaning the same thing as rows are added or removed.
questions.explain: Structured references name a Table's columns directly, e.g. Table1[Sales] or [@Sales] for the current row, removing the need for $ absolute references and keeping formulas valid as the Table grows.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 interface term to what it actually is.
right: Jumps to the edge of a contiguous data region instead of scrolling
Excel's built-in flag that a cell holds a number stored as text
An Excel Table's optional summary row using SUBTOTAL, which ignores filtered-out rows
Shows the current cell's address, or jumps to an address typed into it
questions.explain: The Name Box shows and jumps to cell addresses. Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the edge of a data region. The green triangle flags a text-stored number. A Table's Total row uses SUBTOTAL, so it correctly ignores rows hidden by a filter.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about named ranges and the Name Manager, per Lesson 4.
options: A name must start with a letter or underscore and can't contain spaces or match a real cell reference like Q1
A name's scope can be restricted to a single worksheet instead of the whole workbook
Excel never creates a named range on its own — every name in the Name Manager was typed by hand
A #REF! shown next to a name in the Name Manager means whatever that name used to point at was deleted
Once a name is defined, it can only be used in the worksheet where it was created, regardless of scope settings
questions.explain: Names follow specific character rules and can be scoped to one sheet, and Excel itself auto-creates names when a range becomes a Table — so the claim that every name is typed by hand is false. A #REF! next to a name specifically signals its target was deleted, breaking every formula that uses it. Scope, not the sheet a name happened to be created on, controls where it can be used, so that last statement is also false.

questions.prompt: What is the core structural problem with VLOOKUP that XLOOKUP was specifically built to fix?
options: VLOOKUP can only search the leftmost column of its table array and return a value to the right of it, so it can never look left; XLOOKUP's lookup and return arrays are independent and can point anywhere
VLOOKUP cannot be used inside an Excel Table at all
VLOOKUP can only return numeric values, never text
VLOOKUP requires the source data to be sorted in ascending order before it will run
VLOOKUP cannot be combined with IFERROR or IFNA
VLOOKUP is only available in Excel for the web, not the desktop app
questions.explain: VLOOKUP's lookup column must be the leftmost column of its table array, so it structurally cannot look left — if the value you're searching by sits to the right of the value you want back, VLOOKUP cannot do it without rearranging the data first. XLOOKUP's lookup_array and return_array are independent references, so it can look left or right with no rearrangement.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes an old limitation of VLOOKUP's approximate-match mode (TRUE), which does require sorted data to behave correctly — but that's a separate pitfall tied to the 4th argument, not the leftmost-column limitation XLOOKUP was actually designed around. VLOOKUP's exact-match mode (FALSE) doesn't require sorted data at all.

questions.prompt: This VLOOKUP has no 4th argument. What does that actually mean, and why is it risky against an ID column?
options: range_lookup defaults to TRUE (approximate match), so for an ID that isn't an exact match, it can silently return a plausible-looking but wrong value instead of an error
It defaults to FALSE (exact match), so it's already safe with no changes needed
Excel throws a syntax error immediately because the 4th argument is required
It searches every column of ProductTable for a match, not just the first one
questions.explain: Omitting range_lookup defaults VLOOKUP to approximate match (TRUE). For an exact-match use case like an ID or SKU lookup, that's the single most common cause of a VLOOKUP returning a wrong-but-plausible value with no error at all — the fix is explicitly passing FALSE (or 0).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ returns the position of a value within a range, not the value itself — it has to be wrapped in INDEX to actually retrieve what's stored at that position.
questions.explain: MATCH answers "where" a value lives inside a range as a plain position number; INDEX is what actually fetches the value stored at that position. Neither function alone performs a full lookup.

questions.prompt: RegionCol lists regions down the side of DataGrid and MonthRow lists months across the top. What does this formula actually return?
options: The single value sitting at the intersection of the West row and the March column inside DataGrid
Every value in the West row, spilled across as an array
The word "West" itself, since the first MATCH is evaluated last
An error, because INDEX can't accept two position arguments at once
questions.explain: INDEX(array, row_num, col_num) accepts both a row and a column position. The first MATCH finds which row West lives in, the second finds which column March lives in, and INDEX returns exactly the one cell where those two coordinates meet — a two-way lookup, not two separate single lookups.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about IFERROR and IFNA, per Lesson 8.
options: IFERROR replaces any error type — #N/A, #REF!, #VALUE!, #NAME?, and more — with the same fallback value
IFNA only catches #N/A, letting every other error type display normally
Wrapping a broken lookup in IFERROR makes the underlying problem get fixed faster, since the fallback text draws attention to it
#N/A from a lookup usually means a legitimate "no match found," while #REF! usually means something is actually broken
IFNA and IFERROR always produce identical results for any formula, since both exist only to suppress errors
questions.explain: IFERROR catches every error type indiscriminately, while IFNA catches only #N/A and lets other errors display. That distinction matters because #N/A is usually an expected "no match," while #REF!/#VALUE!/#NAME? usually mean something is genuinely broken — and hiding a broken formula behind the same friendly fallback text as a normal miss means it never gets fixed, the opposite of what the third statement claims.

questions.prompt: A developer wrote this SUMIFS intending to total Sales for the West region in 2024, but it returns an error. What's wrong?
options: SUMIFS puts the range to sum first, then criteria-range/criteria pairs — this formula has the order reversed, putting each criteria value before its range instead of after
SUMIFS can only accept one condition at a time, so adding a second one always fails
"West" needs to be a cell reference, never a typed string, inside SUMIFS
SUMIFS requires every argument to be wrapped in its own set of parentheses
questions.explain: SUMIFS's argument order is sum_range, then criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, and so on — the range to aggregate always comes first, followed by range/criteria pairs in that order. This formula reverses each pair, which is exactly the SUMIF-to-SUMIFS argument-order mixup Lesson 9 calls out as a common mistake.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ returns TRUE only when every condition passed to it is true, while OR only needs one of its conditions to be true.
questions.explain: AND requires every condition to be true to return TRUE; OR only needs one. Mixing the two up is one of the most common silent logic bugs in Excel, since a swapped AND/OR still calculates with no error — it just returns the wrong answer for edge cases.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 3 function to what it actually does.
right: Removes extra spaces, including invisible ones that silently break an exact-match lookup
Returns the last day of a month that is a given number of months away from a start date
Converts a number or date into a formatted display string using a format code
Returns the whole number of complete years, months, or days between two dates — hidden from Excel's autocomplete
questions.explain: EOMONTH finds month-end dates by offset. DATEDIF returns a precise year/month/day duration and still works correctly even though Excel hides it from autocomplete. TEXT formats a value into a display string, which matters specifically when concatenating a formatted number into a sentence. TRIM removes stray spaces, including ones invisible to the eye that break exact-match lookups.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about nested IF versus IFS, per Lessons 10 and 11.
options: A nested IF chain testing the same field against a new threshold in every branch is exactly the pattern IFS was built to replace
IFS evaluates condition/result pairs in order, with no nested parentheses to lose count of
An IFS formula with no final TRUE catch-all pair returns #N/A if nothing else matches
Nested IF is unreadable at any number of levels, even two or three
IFS and nested IF can never produce the same result for the same conditions
questions.explain: IFS exists specifically to flatten the "same field, new threshold every branch" pattern that makes nested IF hard to audit, and it does so with ordered, unnested condition/result pairs. Skip its final TRUE catch-all and it returns #N/A if nothing matches. Nested IF is fine at two or three levels — it only degrades past that — and a well-built IFS and nested IF testing the same conditions return identical results, so the last two statements are both false.

questions.prompt: HireDate is 2019-03-15 and TODAY() is 2026-10-08. What does this formula return, and what does the "Y" argument control?
options: 7 — the number of complete years between the two dates; "Y" selects whole years as the unit
7.6 — a fractional year count; "Y" means "include partial years"
2026 — the year portion of TODAY(); "Y" extracts just the year number
An error, because DATEDIF only works with "D" as the unit
questions.explain: DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit) returns a whole number for the chosen unit — "Y" for complete years, "M" for months, "D" for days. From March 2019 to October 2026 is 7 complete years, since the March anniversary has already passed this year — DATEDIF never returns a decimal.

questions.prompt: A PivotTable is built with its Table/Range pointed at a fixed range, Sheet1!$B$1:$C$50. Next month, 20 new rows of data are added below row 50. What happens to the PivotTable, and why?
options: It doesn't include the new rows until someone manually edits the source range, because a fixed range reference never grows on its own
It automatically includes the new rows the next time it's refreshed, the same as if it were built from a Table
It throws an error the moment new rows are added below the original range
It automatically re-sorts the new rows to the top of the report
questions.explain: A PivotTable built from a raw cell range is fixed at whatever address was selected — it has no way to know rows were added below it, and stays stuck at $B$1:$C$50 until someone manually updates the source reference. A PivotTable built from a real Excel Table instead shows the Table's name and automatically expands as the Table grows, which is exactly why Lesson 13 insists on starting from a Table.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a PivotTable calculated field's formula, like Margin % = Profit/Revenue, operates on the ________ of each field already in the report — not a row-by-row average of already-computed percentages.
questions.explain: A calculated field computes using the aggregated sums already shown for each field — summed Profit divided by summed Revenue — which is mathematically correct at every subtotal level, unlike averaging individual rows' percentages after the fact.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the choice between a PivotTable calculated field and a calculated column on the source data, per Lesson 14.
options: A calculated field's formula only exists inside the one PivotTable it was added to
A calculated column is visible in the raw data and usable by any other formula, chart, or PivotTable built from that Table
A calculated column correctly represents a ratio-of-sums at a subtotal level, the same way a calculated field does
A calculated field changes the underlying source data the moment it's created
The right choice depends on whether other parts of the workbook need the per-row value directly
questions.explain: A calculated field lives only inside its PivotTable and never touches the source data, while a calculated column is visible and reusable everywhere else in the workbook — but a column of per-row percentages, summed or averaged, doesn't equal the true blended ratio-of-sums the way a calculated field's formula does, so that statement is false. The right choice comes down to whether the per-row value is actually needed elsewhere, not whether the field secretly edits the source data, which it never does.

questions.prompt: Match each PivotTable/PivotChart term to what it actually is.
right: An always-visible, click-based filter button set for one field
A control built specifically for date fields, with a drag-to-select range and a Years/Quarters/Months/Days zoom level
Dropdown controls Excel places directly on a PivotChart, unique to PivotCharts
A slicer or Timeline linked to more than one PivotTable sharing the same data source
questions.explain: A slicer is an always-visible button set for one field. A Timeline is a slicer purpose-built for dates, with a drag range and a zoom level. Field buttons are interactive dropdowns Excel places directly on a PivotChart — a capability a standard chart has no equivalent for. A connected slicer or Timeline filters multiple PivotTables (or PivotCharts) at once, as long as they share the same source.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for building a PivotTable that keeps including new data automatically, per Lesson 13.
items: Convert the raw range of data into a real Excel Table with Ctrl+T
Insert a PivotTable with Table/Range pointed at the Table's name, not a fixed cell address
Drag fields into the Rows, Columns, and Values zones to shape the report
Add new rows of data directly beneath the source Table
Refresh the PivotTable and confirm the new rows are already included
questions.explain: Starting from a real Table, not a raw range, is what makes the rest of this sequence work — the PivotTable's Table/Range box then shows the Table's name instead of a fixed address, so once fields are arranged and new rows are added to the Table, a simple refresh picks them up automatically with nothing to manually fix.

questions.prompt: This formula was entered with Ctrl+Shift+Enter in Excel 2016. What happens if the source data in C2:C100 later grows to C2:C150?
options: The formula still only evaluates C2:C100 — a legacy CSE array formula is fixed-size the moment it's entered, and must be reselected and re-entered to cover the new rows
It automatically spills to cover the new rows, exactly like a dynamic array function would
It throws #SPILL! the instant the source data grows
It silently converts itself into a modern dynamic array formula the next time the workbook opens
questions.explain: A legacy array formula entered with Ctrl+Shift+Enter (shown by Excel's automatic curly braces) always returns a fixed-size result decided the moment it was entered. Growing the source range doesn't grow the formula with it — someone has to reselect the range and re-enter it. A modern dynamic array function doesn't have this problem, which is the whole point of the 2018 dynamic array engine.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: typing a spilled formula's top-left cell address followed by ________, like A2#, refers to that formula's entire current result, however big it gets.
questions.explain: The # spill operator means "whatever this spilled array currently contains" — unlike a hardcoded range like A2:A11, it never goes stale if the spill's size changes, because it always refers to the live spill rather than a fixed set of cells.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about FILTER, SORT, and UNIQUE, per Lesson 18.
options: FILTER's include argument must be a boolean condition built from a range the same height as the array being filtered
Leaving out FILTER's if_empty argument means a no-match result throws #CALC! instead of showing blank
SORT's sort_index argument of 1 always refers to the worksheet's column A, regardless of where the sorted array actually starts
UNIQUE's exactly_once argument, set to TRUE, returns only values that appear exactly one time — genuinely different from ordinary distinct values
Nesting SORT(UNIQUE(range)) requires an intermediate helper cell to hold UNIQUE's result before SORT can use it
questions.explain: FILTER's include array must match the data's height, and omitting if_empty causes #CALC! on no matches since Excel can't spill an empty array. UNIQUE's exactly_once mode is genuinely different from plain distinct values — it drops anything with even one duplicate. SORT's sort_index is relative to the array's own first column, not the sheet's column A, so that statement is false; and nesting functions like SORT(UNIQUE(...)) needs no intermediate cell at all, so that statement is also false.

questions.prompt: A SEQUENCE(10) formula in cell A2 suddenly throws #SPILL! after someone typed a value into cell A7, which sits inside where the sequence needs to spill. What's the fastest way to actually find what's blocking it?
options: Click the error indicator on A2 and choose Select Obstructing Cells, which jumps straight to the blocking cell
Delete and re-enter the SEQUENCE formula from scratch, since #SPILL! means the formula itself is broken
Convert the range into an Excel Table, since Tables resolve #SPILL! automatically
Widen column A, since #SPILL! only means the column isn't wide enough to display the result
questions.explain: #SPILL! means Excel calculated a result it couldn't place — something is occupying a cell in its intended spill area. The error indicator's Select Obstructing Cells command jumps straight to exactly what's in the way, which is far faster than guessing. Notably, putting the formula inside a Table would make things worse, not better — Tables don't support spilling at all.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 5 term to what it actually means.
right: A dynamic array's automatic placement of its results into neighboring cells
The error shown when a dynamic array's result can't be placed because something is in its way
Assigns a name to an intermediate value or expression so it's calculated once and reused inside one formula
Returns only values that appear exactly one time in a range, excluding anything with even one duplicate
questions.explain: Spilling is a dynamic array automatically placing its results into neighboring cells. #SPILL! fires when something blocks that placement. LET names an intermediate expression once so it's calculated a single time and reused. UNIQUE's exactly_once argument returns only values with zero duplicates, which is a stricter condition than ordinary distinct values.

questions.prompt: Fundamentally, what is Power Query within Excel?
options: A separate transformation engine — connect, transform, combine, then load — that happens to live inside Excel's ribbon, distinct from formulas or PivotTables
A new category of worksheet formula for cleaning text inside a single cell
A PivotTable variant specialized for combining multiple PivotTables into one
A charting tool for building PivotCharts from multiple data sources at once
A macro-recording feature that only works with VBA-enabled workbooks
A cloud-only service with no offline functionality inside desktop Excel
questions.explain: Power Query is its own transformation engine — Connect, Transform, Combine, Load — that happens to ship inside Excel's Data tab as "Get & Transform." It operates on data before it ever lands in a worksheet, which is why Lesson 21 insists on treating it as a distinct tool rather than an extension of formulas or PivotTables.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes something closer to Append (Lesson 23), which does combine multiple queries' rows into one — but that's one specific operation inside Power Query, not a definition of what Power Query itself fundamentally is. Power Query's scope is the whole four-phase Connect/Transform/Combine/Load engine, not just the combining step.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: clicking ________ re-runs every recorded Applied Step, in order, against the current state of the source data — turning next week's cleanup from a repeat manual chore into one click.
questions.explain: Refresh re-executes a query's entire Applied Steps list against whatever the source data currently looks like, which is the whole value of building a query once instead of manually re-cleaning a fresh export every time it arrives.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about cleaning data in Power Query, per Lesson 22.
options: Remove Duplicates keeps the first occurrence of each unique combination of the selected columns and drops the rest
Which columns are selected before running Remove Duplicates changes what actually counts as a "duplicate"
Splitting a column by delimiter always produces exactly two new columns, no matter how many pieces the delimiter separates
A column's data type icon in the header can be clicked directly to change that column's type
Unchecking (blank) in a column's filter dropdown only removes blank rows for the current session — they reappear on the next refresh
questions.explain: Remove Duplicates keeps the first row of each unique combination of the selected columns, and which columns you pick changes what "duplicate" even means for that data. Splitting by delimiter creates one new column per separated piece, not always exactly two, so that statement is false. The data type icon is directly clickable to change a column's type. And because filtering out blanks is a recorded query step, it survives every refresh rather than needing to be redone — so the last statement is also false.

questions.prompt: You have a January sales export and a February sales export, both with the exact same column layout, and you want one combined table of every row from both months. Which Power Query command is correct, and why?
options: Append — it stacks rows from tables that already share the same columns, the same idea as a UNION
Merge — it joins tables sideways on a shared key column, the same idea as a VLOOKUP for whole tables
Either command works identically here, since both just combine two queries into one
Neither — Power Query can only combine queries that were loaded from the exact same file
questions.explain: The deciding question is whether the tables share a key column to match on, or share the same columns and just need more rows. January and February exports with identical columns need Append, which stacks rows downward like a UNION. Merge is for the opposite situation — a shared key column used to bring in new columns sideways, like a VLOOKUP scaled up to whole tables.

questions.prompt: A report uses a pie chart to show how total monthly revenue changed from January through December. Why is this the wrong chart choice, specifically?
options: A pie chart has no concept of time or order at all, so it can't show a trend — a line chart is built specifically for change over a continuous axis
A pie chart can only display up to three categories at once
A pie chart requires its data to already be sorted alphabetically before it can be built
A pie chart and a line chart are functionally interchangeable, so this is a stylistic choice, not an error
questions.explain: Trend-over-time is a specific question — is a value going up, down, or holding steady across a period — and a pie chart has no sense of order or time to represent that with at all. A line chart exists specifically for change over a continuous axis, which is exactly the question this report is actually trying to answer.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of running Goal Seek in the correct order, for finding the unit price that hits a $50,000 revenue target.
items: Identify the formula cell whose result you care about — here, the Total Revenue formula — as the Set cell
Open Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek
Enter the exact target number, 50000, as the To value
Choose the Unit Price cell that the Total Revenue formula depends on as the By changing cell
Run Goal Seek and confirm Unit Price updated to the value that makes Total Revenue land on exactly $50,000
questions.explain: Every Goal Seek run needs the same three pieces of information — the Set cell holding the formula, the To value as the exact target, and the By changing cell as the one input Goal Seek is allowed to adjust — identified before opening the dialog, entered inside it, and then run to solve backward from the target to the input.
